## TestimonyArguments.SolaGratia — salvation by grace alone

"For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own
doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast"
(Ephesians 2:8–9). Every party to this dispute reads the verse and agrees with
it. That is the first thing to understand about *sola gratia*, "by grace alone",
and the reason the conclusion below is stated with more care than the slogan.

### Everyone says "by grace"

The Council of Trent, answering the Reformers in 1547, taught that "in adults,
the beginning of the said Justification is to be derived from the prevenient
grace of God", the grace that goes before, by which they are called "without
any merits existing on their parts". It quoted Paul: "if it be a grace, it is
not now by works, otherwise … grace is no more grace" (Romans 11:6). The
Remonstrants, the followers of Arminius who petitioned the States of Holland in
1610, called grace "the beginning, continuance, and accomplishment of all good".
Neither is Pelagian. Neither thinks a person can begin to turn to God by their
own power.

So a conclusion stated as "salvation is by grace" would follow from all three
positions and separate none of them. When the Synod of Dort answered the
Remonstrants in 1619, it meant something sharper. The grace that saves brings
about the consent it asks for, rather than waiting on a will that could refuse
it. And the new life is, in the Canons' words, "a making alive, which God works
in us without our aid"; the Westminster Confession says the sinner "is
altogether passive therein, until, being quickened and renewed by the Holy
Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call". The older name for this is
*monergism*, from the Greek for "one at work".

The conclusion here has those three parts. Salvation is by grace; the grace that
saves is effectual of itself; and the will is passive in being made alive. Each
rival holds the first part and denies one of the others.

- **Trent** denies the third. Its fourth canon on justification condemns anyone
  who says that the free will, "moved and excited by God", does not cooperate
  "by assenting to God exciting and calling", but "as something inanimate, …
  is merely passive". The same canon condemns anyone who says the will "cannot
  refuse its consent, if it would".
- **The Remonstrants** deny the second. Their fourth article says that grace "is
  not irresistible, inasmuch as it is written concerning many, that they have
  resisted the Holy Ghost", citing Stephen's charge to the council: "you always
  resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51).

### Two routes to the conclusion

The Reformed case has two routes, called *strands* below, each from a different
text. Each begins from a reading of its text and takes a step from that reading
to the conclusion.

**Ephesians 2.** Paul has just said that his readers "were dead in the trespasses
and sins", and that God "made us alive together with Christ" (2:1, 5). Then:
"by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing".
The Greek word for "this" (τοῦτο) is neuter, while "faith" (πίστις) and "grace"
(χάρις) are both feminine, so the pronoun does not point to either word on its
own. Hoehner and Robertson read it as pointing to the whole of being saved by
grace through faith. The strand then takes two steps: since faith is part of
that whole, faith is God's gift; and since it is given to people who were dead
until God made them alive, the turning is his work alone.

**Romans 9.** "So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who
has mercy" (Romans 9:16). Read as being about God's mercy in saving, and not
only about his choice of a people for a part in history, the verse says that
receiving mercy does not hang on anyone's willing. The Romans strand does not
use the Ephesians grammar at all.

### What the machine finds

Lean checks, for each position written as a list of premises, whether the
conclusion follows. It does not check whether the premises are true.

The Reformed premises reach the conclusion, and neither rival's do, though both
reach its first part. A reading is called *load-bearing* when removing it, with
everything else kept, stops the conclusion following. Neither reading is
load-bearing alone, because each strand reaches the conclusion without the other.
Removed together they are, so the Reformed case needs one of the two readings,
and either will do.

The readings, though, are not where the rivals part from it. Robertson reads
"this" exactly as Hoehner does, and draws the opposite lesson: the whole act of
being saved is "conditioned on faith on our part". Calvin, on the next verse,
writes that Paul's "meaning is, not that faith is the gift of God, but that
salvation is given to us by God". So the step from the pronoun to faith as a gift
is rated *disputed*: a reader the library cites grants its grounds and denies its
conclusion.

The next step is disputed too. Arminius acknowledged faith to be God's "benefit
and gift", and ascribed to grace "the commencement, the continuance and the
consummation of all good". He could grant everything the Ephesians strand rests
on, up to its last step. He refused that step, believing "that many persons
resist the Holy Spirit and reject the grace that is offered". Dort's answer is
its article on faith, which it calls the gift of God "not on account of its
being offered by God to man, to be accepted or rejected at his pleasure, but
because it is in reality conferred". The difference between the two is the
difference between those two senses of *gift*, and the grammar of the verse
does not decide it (`gift_of_faith_does_not_settle_resistibility`).

Romans goes the same way. Arminius read Romans 9 as being about salvation, "not
to him that worketh, but to him that believeth". Abasciano, who reads its
election as of a people rather than of individuals, still grants that "Paul's
argument in Romans 9 surely concerns the salvation of Israel". The reading is
widely granted. It is the step from it to God's work alone that Arminius denies.

Trent's canon has the same feature at both its halves. That the will "cannot
refuse its consent, if it would" is condemned, which seems to deny that grace is
effectual of itself. But Aquinas held both that if God moves the will, "it is
incompatible with this supposition, that the will be not moved thereto. But it
is not impossible simply", and that the man God moves to grace "will infallibly
attain to it". And the canon's "cooperates" speaks of the will "disposing and
preparing itself" for justification, while Aquinas and Dort both place the
will's own activity after a first moment in which it "is moved and does not
move". So both of Trent's steps are rated disputed.

### What is not encoded

Aquinas and the Thomist school are cited here for two ratings, and are not a
position of their own. They hold that grace is infallibly effectual, and Aquinas
puts the infusion of grace first "in the order of nature", before "the
free-will's movement towards God". Whether they reach the sharpened conclusion,
and where they part from Dort if they do not, is a question this module does
not ask.

John 6:44 ("No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him") is
the third text most often cited for the Reformed view, and is not encoded
either. Nor is election, the subject of the first of the Remonstrants' articles,
which is a dispute of its own.

## TestimonyArguments.SolaGratia.Atoms — the atomic claims

Sixteen claims, in four groups: the texts every party reads, the readings of
them that are in dispute, the claims Trent and the Remonstrants add, and the
three parts of the conclusion.

The conclusion has three parts so that a rival can hold one part and deny
another, and both rivals do. Everyone in this dispute says that salvation is by
grace and not earned. Only the Reformed say that grace brings about the consent
it asks for, and that in being made alive the will contributes nothing.

## TestimonyArguments.SolaGratia.Sources — citation and classification for every atom

`cite` is total, so an uncited atom does not compile. The three positions agree
about the texts and disagree about what they mean, so each has its own `cite`,
sharing `baseCite` for the texts and the conclusion. Each package's list of
sources then names the people who hold its premises: the Remonstrant reading of
Acts 7:51 cites the Remonstrants, and the Reformed denial of it cites Dort.

Dort and the Remonstrance are cited from Schaff's *Creeds of Christendom*,
which prints both; Trent from Tanner's *Decrees*; Arminius from Nichols's
translation of his works.

#### Ratings for inference steps

A step's rating is its own, cited to whoever grants its grounds and denies its
conclusion, or, where no one was found who does, to whoever grants both.

<a id="graceInference"></a>
**`graceInference`**

The rating of the step from Romans 11:6 to "salvation is by grace":
`consensus`. Trent quotes the verse to that effect, "if it be a grace, it is not
now by works" (Session VI, chapter 8); the Remonstrants' fourth article calls
grace "the beginning, continuance, and accomplishment of all good"; Dort says
that conversion "must be wholly ascribed to God" (III/IV, article 10).

```lean
def graceInference : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work tannerDecrees
        (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Trent, Session VI (1547), ch. 8"),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work schaffCreeds3
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Five Arminian Articles (1610), art. 4"),
        Reference.work schaffCreeds3
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Canons of Dort, III/IV, art. 10")],
    tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
    confidence := Confidence.consensus }
```

<a id="ephesiansInference"></a>
**`ephesiansInference`**

**The rating of the step from "this" pointing to the whole, to "faith is
God's gift": `disputed`.** Robertson grants the ground and denies the conclusion:
"this" refers "not to [pistis] (feminine) or to [charis] (feminine also), but to
the act of being saved by grace conditioned on faith on our part". Calvin, on
the next verse, says the same of "the gift of God": "His meaning is, not that
faith is the gift of God, but that salvation is given to us by God."

```lean
def ephesiansInference : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work robertsonWordPictures4
        (Bib.Locus.adLoc { book := Book.ephesians, chapter := 2, verse := 8 }),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work calvinGalatiansEphesians (Bib.Locus.pages 228 229)],
    tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
    confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="giftInference"></a>
**`giftInference`**

**The rating of the step from the gift to God's work alone: `disputed`.**
Arminius grants both grounds. Faith is God's gift: he speaks of God, "whose
benefit and gift I acknowledge faith to be" (*Apology*, article 4). And a man
cannot turn to God by himself: he ascribes to grace "the commencement, the
continuance and the consummation of all good". He denies the conclusion: "many
persons resist the Holy Spirit and reject the grace that is offered"
(*Declaration of Sentiments*).

```lean
def giftInference : Source :=
  { primary := Reference.work arminiusWorks1 (Bib.Locus.page 600),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work arminiusWorks1 (Bib.Locus.page 681),
        Reference.work schaffCreeds3
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Five Arminian Articles (1610), art. 4")],
    tradition := Tradition.arminian, confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="romansInference"></a>
**`romansInference`**

**The rating of the step from Romans 9:16, read as being about salvation, to
God's work alone: `disputed`.** Arminius grants the ground: the chapter's theme
is "That the Gospel, not the law, is the power of God unto salvation, not to him
that worketh, but to him that believeth", and the willing and running of 9:16 is
the effort by which a man "hopes that he will obtain justification and salvation
apart from the mercy of God". He denies the conclusion: the mercy goes to those
"who seek righteousness and salvation by faith in Christ", and grace can be
refused.

```lean
def romansInference : Source :=
  { primary := Reference.work arminiusWorks3 (Bib.Locus.pages 527 565),
    tradition := Tradition.arminian, confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="cooperationInference"></a>
**`cooperationInference`**

**The rating of Trent's step from cooperation to "the will is not passive":
`disputed`, and the dissent rests on a distinction.** Canon 4 speaks of the will
"disposing and preparing itself" for justification. Aquinas grants that grace
works with a will that moves, which he calls cooperating grace, and still holds
that in grace's first effect "our mind is moved and does not move, but … God is
the sole mover" (I-II q.111 a.2). Dort likewise grants that the renewed will
"becomes itself active" (III/IV, article 12). Both place the will's activity
after a first moment in which it is only moved; the canon does not say which
moment it means.

```lean
def cooperationInference : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work aquinasSumma (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "I-II q.111 a.2"),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work schaffCreeds3
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Canons of Dort, III/IV, art. 12"),
        Reference.work tannerDecrees
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 4")],
    tradition := Tradition.romanCatholic, confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="dissentInference"></a>
**`dissentInference`**

**The rating of Trent's step from "the will can refuse" to "grace is not
effectual of itself": `disputed`.** Aquinas grants the ground and denies the
conclusion. "If God moves the will to anything, it is incompatible with this
supposition, that the will be not moved thereto. But it is not impossible
simply" (I-II q.10 a.4 ad 3). And "if God intends, while moving, that the one
whose heart He moves should attain to grace, he will infallibly attain to it"
(I-II q.112 a.3). On that reading the will can refuse, taken simply, and grace
is effectual all the same.

```lean
def dissentInference : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work aquinasSumma (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "I-II q.10 a.4 ad 3"),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work aquinasSumma (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "I-II q.112 a.3"),
        Reference.work tannerDecrees
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 4")],
    tradition := Tradition.romanCatholic, confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="resistanceInference"></a>
**`resistanceInference`**

The rating of the Remonstrants' step from Acts 7:51 to "grace is not
effectual of itself": `wellSupported`. Grant that what Stephen's hearers resisted
was the grace that saves, and no reader was found who denies that grace can
then be resisted. Reformed readers deny the ground instead: John Gill reads the

```lean
    supporting := [Reference.work arminiusWorks1 (Bib.Locus.page 600)],
    tradition := Tradition.arminian, confidence := Confidence.wellSupported }
```

## TestimonyArguments.SolaGratia.Lines — the inference steps and the lines of reason

Two routes reach the conclusion, one through Ephesians 2 and one through
Romans 9, and each has a reading of its text that is in dispute. A third line,
from Romans 11:6, delivers only the first part of the conclusion, that
salvation is by grace, and every party walks it: Trent quotes the verse in the
eighth chapter of its decree on justification.

Trent and the Remonstrants each deny a different part of what the Reformed
lines deliver, so each has lines of its own here. Trent's fourth canon on
justification denies that the will is merely passive, and in the same sentence
says the will can refuse if it wishes. The Remonstrants deny that grace cannot
be resisted, from Stephen's speech in Acts 7.

#### The conclusion

<a id="solaGratia"></a>
**`solaGratia`**

**Sola gratia, stated sharply enough that the rivals divide from it.**
Salvation is by grace and not earned; the grace that saves brings about the
consent it seeks; and in being made alive the will contributes nothing. The
three parts are separate claims so that a rival can be shown holding the first
and denying the others, which is what both rivals do.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{#claim-14}{P_{14}} \land \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}} \land \href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\)

</div>

#### The steps

<a id="graceStep"></a>
**`graceStep`**

Romans 11:6: if salvation is by grace it is not by works, so it is by grace
and not earned.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{#claim-4}{P_{4}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) — *would give:* Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act

</div>

<a id="ephesiansStep"></a>
**`ephesiansStep`**

Ephesians 2:8–9, with "this" read as pointing to the whole of being saved
by grace through faith: so faith, part of that whole, is God's gift. Rated
`disputed`: Robertson reads the pronoun the same way and calls the whole
"conditioned on faith on our part", and Calvin, on the next verse, writes "not
that faith is the gift of God, but that salvation is given to us by God".

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{#claim-7}{P_{7}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would give:* Faith itself is God's gift, not something the believer adds

</div>

<a id="giftStep"></a>
**`giftStep`**

**The step Arminius refuses.** If faith is God's gift, and it is given to
those who were dead until God made them alive (Ephesians 2:1–5), then
conversion is God's work alone. Rated `disputed`: Arminius grants both grounds
and denies that the gift cannot be refused. Dort's answer is its article on
faith: God's gift "not on account of its being offered by God to man, to be
accepted or rejected at his pleasure, but because it is in reality conferred"
(III/IV, article 14).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{#claim-9}{P_{9}} \land \href{#claim-1}{P_{1}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* Conversion is God's work alone: grace brings about the sinner's consent

</div>

<a id="romansStep"></a>
**`romansStep`**

Romans 9:16, read as being about salvation: if God's saving mercy "depends
not on human will or exertion", conversion is God's work alone. Rated
`disputed`: Arminius grants that the verse is about salvation and reads its
willing and running as seeking salvation by the works of the law, so that the
mercy goes to believers and can be refused.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \land \href{#claim-8}{P_{8}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* Conversion is God's work alone: grace brings about the sinner's consent

</div>

<a id="monergismUnpacked"></a>
**`monergismUnpacked`**

What "God's work alone" means, unpacked into the conclusion's second and
third parts: grace brings about the consent, and the will contributes nothing
to its own new life.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}} \land \href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — *would give:* \\(\href{#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks; \\(\href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) In being made alive the will is passive, and contributes nothing to it

</div>

<a id="cooperationStep"></a>
**`cooperationStep`**

**Trent's fourth canon, first half.** The will, moved by God, cooperates by
assenting, as "Return to me" calls on it to; so it is not passive. Rated
`disputed`: Aquinas grants that grace cooperates with a will that moves and
holds that in grace's first effect the mind "is moved and does not move".

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{#claim-11}{P_{11}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — *would deny:* In being made alive the will is passive, and contributes nothing to it

</div>

<a id="dissentStep"></a>
**`dissentStep`**

**Trent's fourth canon, second half.** The will, moved by God, can refuse
if it wishes; so grace is not effectual of itself. Rated `disputed`: Aquinas
grants that a will God moves could, taken simply, fail to be moved, and still
holds that the man God moves to grace attains it infallibly.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\(\href{#claim-12}{P_{12}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — *would deny:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks

</div>

<a id="resistanceStep"></a>
**`resistanceStep`**

**The Remonstrants' fourth article.** Stephen's hearers resisted the Holy
Spirit, and what they resisted was the grace that saves; so that grace is not
effectual of itself.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- \\((\href{#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{#claim-10}{P_{10}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — *would deny:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks

</div>

#### The lines

<a id="graceLine"></a>
**`graceLine`** — Romans 11:6 (by grace, so not by works)

**Romans 11:6**, the line every party walks. It delivers the first part of
the conclusion and nothing more.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-4}{P_{4}}\\) — Romans 11:6 — if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-4}{P_{4}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) — *at issue:* Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act

</div>

<a id="ephesiansLine"></a>
**`ephesiansLine`** — Ephesians 2:8–9 ("this is not your own doing")

**Ephesians 2:8–9**, read with "this" pointing to the whole of being saved by
grace through faith. It delivers that faith is God's gift, which is not yet the
conclusion.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — Ephesians 2:8–9 — by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-7}{P_{7}}\\) — In Ephesians 2:8, "this" (τοῦτο) points to the whole of being saved by grace through faith
- (3) \\((\href{#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{#claim-7}{P_{7}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *at issue:* Faith itself is God's gift, not something the believer adds

</div>

<a id="giftLine"></a>
**`giftLine`** — Faith given to the dead (Ephesians 2:1–5)

**From the gift to the dead to God's work alone.** Its ground is
Ephesians 2:1–5; the gift is carried in by `ephesiansLine`.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) — Ephesians 2:1–5 — dead in trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ
- (2) \\((\href{#claim-9}{P_{9}} \land \href{#claim-1}{P_{1}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *at issue:* Conversion is God's work alone: grace brings about the sinner's consent

</div>

<a id="romansLine"></a>

- (2) \\(\href{#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) — Romans 9:16 is about God's mercy in saving, not only in choosing a people for history
- (3) \\((\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \land \href{#claim-8}{P_{8}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\)

## TestimonyArguments.SolaGratia.Packages — the positions, and the variants the results ask about

The rivals come first, because they were written first. Each is a position as
its own documents state it: Trent from the sixth session's decree and canons on
justification, the Remonstrants from their five articles of 1610 and from
Arminius. Neither is Pelagian. Both say, in so many words, that salvation is by
grace, and both packages carry the line from Romans 11:6 that delivers it.

The variants after the Reformed package each change one thing, named, so that a
result about a variant is a result about that one change.

#### The rivals

<a id="tridentine"></a>
**`tridentine`** — Trent (Session VI, canon 4)

**Trent**, from the sixth session (1547). Romans 11:6, which its eighth
chapter quotes; Zechariah 1:3 read with Lamentations 5:21, as its fifth chapter
reads them; and canon 4, on the will that cooperates by assenting and can refuse
if it wishes.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-4}{P_{4}}\\) — Romans 11:6 — if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-6}{P_{6}}\\) — Zechariah 1:3 ("return to me, and I will return to you") with Lamentations 5:21 ("restore us to yourself, O Lord")
- (3) \\(\href{#claim-11}{P_{11}}\\) — The free will, moved by God, cooperates by assenting to God's call
- (4) \\(\href{#claim-12}{P_{12}}\\) — The free will, moved by God, can refuse its assent if it wishes
- (5) \\(\href{#claim-4}{P_{4}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) — *would give:* Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act
- (6) \\((\href{#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{#claim-11}{P_{11}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — *would deny:* In being made alive the will is passive, and contributes nothing to it
- (7) \\(\href{#claim-12}{P_{12}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — *would deny:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-14}{P_{14}} \land \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}} \land \href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — *at issue:* \\(\href{#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act; \\(\href{#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks; \\(\href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) In being made alive the will is passive, and contributes nothing to it

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Romans 11:6 — if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works.

<a id="remonstrant"></a>
**`remonstrant`** — Remonstrant (the Five Articles, 1610)

**The Remonstrants**, from their articles of 1610 and from Arminius.
Romans 11:6; the fourth article, that grace is not irresistible, from Acts 7:51;
and what Arminius grants of the Reformed case: the texts of Ephesians 2, that
faith is God's gift, and that Romans 9:16 is about salvation. What is left out
is the two steps from those to God's work alone, which are the steps he
refuses.

- (4) \\(\href{#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) — Ephesians 2:1–5 — dead in trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ
- (5) \\(\href{#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — Ephesians 2:8–9 — by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God

- (8) \\(\href{#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) — Romans 9:16 is about God's mercy in saving, not only in choosing a people for history
- (9) \\(\href{#claim-4}{P_{4}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) — *would give:* Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act
- (10) \\((\href{#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{#claim-10}{P_{10}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — *would deny:* The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-14}{P_{14}} \land \href{#claim-15}{P_{15}} \land \href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — *at issue:* \\(\href{#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) Salvation is by grace and not earned: grace goes before every saving act; \\(\href{#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) The grace that saves brings about the consent it seeks; \\(\href{#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) In being made alive the will is passive, and contributes nothing to it

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Romans 11:6 — if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works, Acts 7:51 — you always resist the Holy Spirit, Ephesians 2:1–5 — dead in trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ, Ephesians 2:8–9 — by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, Romans 9:16 — it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.

- (9) \\((\href{#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{#claim-7}{P_{7}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would give:* Faith itself is God's gift, not something the believer adds
- (10) \\((\href{#claim-9}{P_{9}} \land \href{#claim-1}{P_{1}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — *would give:* Conversion is God's work alone: grace brings about the sinner's consent

## TestimonyArguments.SolaGratia.Results — what does and does not follow

The results come in three groups. The first is what each position reaches: the
Reformed premises reach sola gratia, neither rival's do, and both rivals reach
its first part. The second is which reading of the texts the Reformed case
depends on: neither alone, and the two together. The third is where Arminius
parts from the Ephesians strand, which is after the grammar of "this" and after
faith is granted to be God's gift.

#### The positions

<a id="reformed_establishes"></a>
**`reformed_establishes`**

**Grant the Reformed premises, and sola gratia follows.** The premises are
Romans 11:6; Ephesians 2, with "this" pointing to the whole of being saved by
grace through faith; Romans 9:16, read as being about salvation; the steps from
each of those to God's work alone; and Dort's answer to Acts 7:51. The result
does not say that the readings or the steps are right, only that the conclusion
follows from them. Three of the steps are rated `disputed`, each on a reader who
grants its grounds and denies its conclusion.

```lean
theorem reformed_establishes : Establishes reformed
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="trentsReading"></a>
**`trentsReading`**

Trent's reading, written down: salvation is by grace, the will cooperates
and can refuse, so grace is not effectual of itself and the will is not passive
in being made alive.

```lean
def trentsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.conversionIsGodsWorkAlone => False
    | Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself => False
    | Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="tridentine_not_establishes"></a>
**`tridentine_not_establishes`**

**Trent's premises do not lead to sola gratia.** On Trent's account the will,
moved by God, cooperates by assenting and can refuse its consent; so the second
and third parts of the conclusion fail. Whether canon 4 really denies the second
part is itself disputed, because Aquinas holds both that the will can refuse,
taken simply, and that the man God moves to grace attains it infallibly; that
dispute is in the rating of the canon's step, not in this result.

```lean
theorem tridentine_not_establishes : ¬Establishes tridentine
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="arminiusReading"></a>
**`arminiusReading`**

Arminius's reading, written down: salvation is by grace, faith is God's gift,
Romans 9:16 is about salvation, and the grace that saves can be refused.

```lean
def arminiusReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.conversionIsGodsWorkAlone => False
    | Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself => False
    | Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="remonstrant_not_establishes"></a>
**`remonstrant_not_establishes`**

**The Remonstrants' premises do not lead to sola gratia either**, though they
grant much of what the Reformed case rests on: that faith is God's gift, given
to those dead in sin, and that Romans 9:16 is about salvation. What they add is
their fourth article, that grace is not irresistible, read from Acts 7:51; what
they leave out is the two steps from those grants to God's work alone.

```lean
theorem remonstrant_not_establishes : ¬Establishes remonstrant
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="rivals_hold_salvation_by_grace"></a>
**`rivals_hold_salvation_by_grace`**

**Both rivals reach the first part: salvation is by grace.** Trent's premises
deliver it, and so do the Remonstrants', by the same line from Romans 11:6. A
conclusion stated only as "salvation is by grace" would be established by all
three positions and would divide none of them, which is why the conclusion here
has two further parts.

```lean
theorem rivals_hold_salvation_by_grace : Entails tridentine.premises (p
    Claim.salvationIsByGrace) ∧ Entails remonstrant.premises (p
    Claim.salvationIsByGrace)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="trent_denies_passivity"></a>
**`trent_denies_passivity`**

**Trent's premises deny the third part: the will is not passive.** Canon 4
condemns anyone who says the will "is merely passive", and the premises deliver
the denial outright. The step is rated `disputed`, because the canon speaks of
the will preparing itself for justification and the Reformed claim is about the
moment of being made alive.

```lean
theorem trent_denies_passivity : Entails tridentine.premises (notP
    Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="remonstrants_deny_effectual_grace"></a>
**`remonstrants_deny_effectual_grace`**

**The Remonstrants' premises deny the second part: grace can be resisted.**

```lean
theorem remonstrants_deny_effectual_grace : Entails remonstrant.premises (notP
    Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Which reading the Reformed case depends on

<a id="touto_not_load_bearing"></a>
**`touto_not_load_bearing`**

**The case does not depend on the reading of "this".** Remove the reading on
which "this" in Ephesians 2:8 points to the whole of being saved by grace
through faith, keep everything else, and sola gratia still follows by
Romans 9:16. That is because the Romans strand does not use the Ephesians
grammar, not because the reading is weak; Hoehner and Robertson both hold it.

```lean
theorem touto_not_load_bearing : Establishes reformedWithoutTouto
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romans_reading_not_load_bearing"></a>
**`romans_reading_not_load_bearing`**

**Nor on the reading of Romans 9:16.** Remove the reading on which the verse
is about salvation, keep everything else, and sola gratia still follows by
Ephesians 2.

```lean
theorem romans_reading_not_load_bearing : Establishes
    reformedWithoutRomansReading
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="neitherReadingGranted"></a>
**`neitherReadingGranted`**

The reading on which neither of the two readings holds: "this" in
Ephesians 2:8 does not point to the whole, and Romans 9:16 is about God's choice
of a people for a part in history. Everything else the Reformed position grants
is kept, Dort's answer to Acts 7:51 included.

```lean
def neitherReadingGranted : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.toutoRefersToTheWhole => False
    | Claim.romans9_16ConcernsSalvation => False
    | Claim.faithIsGodsGift => False
    | Claim.conversionIsGodsWorkAlone => False
    | Claim.graceIsEffectualOfItself => False
    | Claim.willIsPassiveInRegeneration => False
    | Claim.acts7_51ResistsSavingGrace => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="readings_jointly_load_bearing"></a>
**`readings_jointly_load_bearing`**

**The two readings together carry it.** Remove both, keep every text and
every step, and sola gratia no longer follows: nothing is left that reaches
God's work alone. So the Reformed case needs at least one of the two readings,
and either will do.

```lean
theorem readings_jointly_load_bearing : ¬Establishes
    reformedWithoutEitherReading
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="ephesians_strand_establishes"></a>
**`ephesians_strand_establishes`**

**The Ephesians strand, argued alone, reaches sola gratia.** It rests on two
steps, both rated `disputed`: from "this" to faith as God's gift, and from the
gift to God's work alone.

```lean
theorem ephesians_strand_establishes : Establishes ephesiansStrand
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romans_strand_establishes"></a>
**`romans_strand_establishes`**

**So does the Romans strand**, on one step rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem romans_strand_establishes : Establishes romansStrand
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Where Arminius parts from the Ephesians strand

<a id="gift_of_faith_does_not_settle_resistibility"></a>
**`gift_of_faith_does_not_settle_resistibility`**

**That faith is God's gift does not settle whether grace can be refused.**
Grant everything the Ephesians strand rests on short of its last step: the
texts, "this" pointing to the whole, and so faith as God's gift, given to those
who were dead in sin. Leave out only the step from that gift to God's work
alone, and sola gratia does not follow. Arminius holds as much as this, and the
countermodel is his reading. Where he parts from the strand is after the
grammar of the pronoun and after the gift.

```lean
theorem gift_of_faith_does_not_settle_resistibility : ¬Establishes
    ephesiansWithoutTheGiftStep
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Satisfiability

`Entails` holds vacuously of premises with no model, so every package carrying
an `Establishes` result is shown to have one. These are claims about the health
of the encoding, not about the dispute, and are not headline results.

<a id="dortReading"></a>
**`dortReading`**

Dort's reading: every claim of the Reformed position holds, and what
Stephen's hearers resisted was the preached word, not the grace that saves.

```lean
def dortReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.acts7_51ResistsSavingGrace => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="reformed_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`reformed_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed package has a model.

```lean
theorem reformed_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable reformed.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="reformedWithoutTouto_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`reformedWithoutTouto_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed package without its reading of "this" has a model.

```lean
theorem reformedWithoutTouto_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    reformedWithoutTouto.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="reformedWithoutRomansReading_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`reformedWithoutRomansReading_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed package without its reading of Romans 9:16 has a model.

```lean
theorem reformedWithoutRomansReading_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    reformedWithoutRomansReading.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="ephesiansStrand_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`ephesiansStrand_is_satisfiable`**

The Ephesians strand alone has a model.

```lean
theorem ephesiansStrand_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable ephesiansStrand.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romansStrand_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`romansStrand_is_satisfiable`**

The Romans strand alone has a model.

```lean
theorem romansStrand_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable romansStrand.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```
